volumes.title: The Ledger Changes Hands
volumes.text:
Entered: one pull-along duck. For: Pip Arkle, aged four. Price: ninepence.

This ledger belonged to my uncle, Osric Thrupp, who made toys in Candle Lane for forty years under the Sign of the Spinning Top. In the autumn he retired to the Grey Coast to look at boats, and left me the shop, the lathe and this book. I am Marigold Thrupp, a cabinet-maker by training. I can make a drawer that shuts. Children, I find, do not want drawers. Inside the cover he has written one rule: Never sell a toy you have not played with. Down the margins he has inked small circles against some orders, and explained nothing.

My first duck came off the bench looking like a boot. I pulled it up and down the shop, as the rule requires. Pip’s grandmother winced. Pip named it Boot and carried it out under his arm.

volumes.title: A Top for Mrs Venn
volumes.text:
Entered: one whipping top, beech, with a red stripe. For: Mrs Venn of Ropewalk Cottages, aged eighty-one. Price: fourpence.

I keep the ledger at Thrupp’s toy shop in Candle Lane, which was my uncle Osric’s until he retired and is now, alarmingly, mine. Mrs Venn came in on two sticks and asked for a top like the one she had at seven. It had a red stripe, she said, and it hummed. My first three fell over. The fourth walked off the counter. A top must weigh the same all the way round, and wood is never as even as it looks. The seventh stood up and hummed.

Uncle’s rule says a toy must be played with before it is sold, so I whipped it round the shop floor till I was breathless. Mrs Venn watched from the chair, then took the whip and did it properly.

volumes.title: Nine Skittles and a King
volumes.text:
Entered: one set of skittles, nine and a king. For: the three Dray brothers at the ferry house. Price: one shilling and sixpence.

Their father ordered them. He ferries people over the Ember all day and would like one evening in which nobody shouts. His sons quarrel over whose turn it is. I am Marigold Thrupp, new to toymaking, and I have no cure for brothers. I painted three skittles blue, three green and three yellow, one colour to a boy, and left the king plain. Then I bowled at them along the shop floor, as my uncle’s rule in the front of this ledger demands. The king is hard to knock down, which seems right.

While the paint dried I counted the little circles Uncle Osric inked in his margins. More than half his orders have one. Mr Dray’s own boyhood toys have three between them.

volumes.title: A Farmyard by Instalments
volumes.text:
Entered: one farmyard, twelve animals and a gate. For: Nell Sorrel of Mill Lane, aged six, in bed with a cough. Price: two shillings.

Nell is to stay indoors till the cough goes, and her mother wanted something to last the month. I make toys at Thrupp’s in Candle Lane, the shop my uncle left me, and I am slow, which for once was useful. The animals arrive one at a time. Every third morning the baker’s boy carries one up on top of the loaves.

The cow went first, then two sheep that really look like sheep. I walked each along the windowsill first, since the rule in this ledger says I must play with whatever I sell. The pig is a difficulty. It will not look like a pig from the front. Nell sends word that she likes the pig best. She has named it Cushion.

volumes.title: A Boat for the Ember
volumes.text:
Entered: one sailing boat, eleven inches, tarred below the waterline. For: Tam Holloway, the bargeman’s boy, aged nine. Price: one shilling.

Tam knows boats. He said, kindly, that my first attempt would turn turtle. It did, twice, in the rain barrel behind the shop. I am Marigold Thrupp, a cabinet-maker by training and a toymaker by inheritance, and nobody had told me about keels. The second boat has lead in its belly, begged from the glazier.

My uncle’s rule, in the front of this ledger, says never to sell a toy you have not played with. So on Thursday I shut the shop and took the boat down to the Ember on a string. I meant to stay ten minutes, and felt foolish for about that long. Then the wind found the sail. I stayed till dusk, and was late with the Sorrels’ farmyard gate.

volumes.title: What the Circles Mean
volumes.text:
Entered: mending, one wooden drummer, left arm off. For: Bessie Fenn, aged five. Price: twopence.

Her father the cooper carried it in. It had been his own, made at this bench by my uncle Osric Thrupp thirty years ago. I looked it up in the ledger. There was the order in Uncle’s hand, with two inked circles beside it. I asked Mr Fenn what they might mean. He laughed. One for the leg he broke off at six, he supposed, and one for the drumstick the dog ate.

So that is the secret of the margins. A circle marks a toy that came back broken. I went through the book tonight and there are hundreds. I had thought my uncle a careful workman. I am Marigold Thrupp, six months in his shop, and I have no circles at all. I intend to keep my own margins perfectly clean.

volumes.title: A Jumping Jack, Privately
volumes.text:
Entered: one jumping jack, painted as a sailor. For: a nephew of Mr Lobb, the toll-keeper on the Lowlands road. Price: sixpence, in exact coin.

Mr Lobb is the gravest man in Emberwick. He counts carts for a living and has never been seen to hurry. He came into Thrupp’s toy shop, where I, Marigold Thrupp, keep this ledger, looked at every shelf in turn, and said the nephew was a serious child who would want something plain. I made the sailor and pulled its string a good many times, as my uncle’s rule requires. Mr Lobb pulled it once at the counter. Then again. He put it inside his coat rather than in his bag.

The carrier says Mr Lobb’s one sister has no children. He adds that something now hangs in the toll-house window and waves at the carts. I have entered the nephew anyway.

volumes.title: The Doll With No Face
volumes.text:
Entered: one wooden doll, nine inches, the face left blank. For: Ottilie Marsh, aged seven. Price: one shilling and threepence.

Ottilie gave her instructions standing on the box I keep for short customers at Thrupp’s in Candle Lane. A painted doll smiles all day, she said, whatever has happened, and she could not be doing with that. She would decide the face each morning. After a week’s thought I painted the head with the black my uncle used for toy slates, and put a stick of chalk and a scrap of flannel in the box.

The rule in the front of this ledger says I must play with every toy first. So the doll spent Tuesday surprised, Wednesday cross, and Thursday, when the varnish on her boots would not dry, extremely patient. Ottilie came on Friday and drew one eyebrow up. She has not told me the doll’s name.

volumes.title: The Horse on the Shelf
volumes.text:
Entered: one hobby horse, ash pole, leather ears. For: Corin Pellow at the Mill House, aged five. Price: two shillings.

I carried it up myself, being Marigold Thrupp, toymaker, and also the shop’s only errand boy. In the nursery, on a high shelf, stood a rocking horse, dapple grey, every hair of its tail in place. I knew it from this ledger: my uncle Osric made it for Mrs Pellow when she was small. She had never been allowed to ride it, she said proudly. It was kept for best. It was as good as new.

There is no circle against that horse in the margin. I had been counting such clean entries as my uncle’s successes. Corin took the hobby horse straight through the yard into the mill stream. I walked back to Candle Lane slowly, and sat a long while looking at the circles.

volumes.title: A Rattle in a Hurry
volumes.text:
Entered: one rattle, sycamore, with dried peas. For: the Garlick baby, not yet named, aged one day. Price: one cottage loaf, still warm.

Mr Garlick the baker hammered on the door of Thrupp’s toy shop at seven with flour to his elbows. The baby had come three weeks early and nothing was ready. Could I make a rattle by noon. I am not quick. But a rattle is a small thing: turned in one piece, sanded until a cheek could find no fault with it, and left unpainted, since it will be chewed.

My uncle’s rule, in the front of this ledger, says to play with every toy before I sell it. I shook the rattle all the way to the bakery, and three dogs and the curate looked round. They are calling her Hester. I ate the loaf at the bench and entered it as paid in full.

volumes.title: Uncle Osric Inspects
volumes.text:
Entered: one whistle, elder wood. For: Mr Osric Thrupp, retired toymaker. Price: refused.

My uncle came up from the Grey Coast by carrier to see what I had done to his shop. He spent the afternoon playing with the stock. He bowled the skittles, sailed a boat in the rain barrel, and timed a top on the counter by the church clock. Then he sat down with this ledger and read my year, from the duck called Boot onward. On each page he ran his thumb down the margin, where he has hundreds of little circles and I have none. Hm, he said. Early days. I took it for praise, though I am no longer sure it was.

He asked for a whistle for the road home, a toy with one job. I played it first, badly. He played it away down Candle Lane, and it was a tune.

volumes.title: The First Circle
volumes.text:
Entered: mending, one pull-along duck, one wheel gone. For: Pip Arkle, aged five. Price: nothing.

Boot came home today. It was my first toy at Thrupp’s, a year ago, when Uncle Osric left me his shop and this ledger. It looked like a boot then and looks worse now. The beak has no paint left, and Pip says it has been through every puddle in Candle Lane and once, briefly, down the well. He stood at the bench while I fitted a wheel, then pulled Boot twice round the shop.

I turned to my first page and inked a circle in the margin, the mark my uncle set against hundreds of his own orders. I had its meaning wrong all year. It marks a toy used hard enough to break. Under his rule in the cover I have added my own line: And be glad when it comes back.

volumes.title: The Baker’s Breath
volumes.text:
There are twelve winds at Emberwick, and I have made something for each. I am Bellwether Tansy. I have kept the kite shed on Whin Hill for forty-odd years, and I am writing this handbook for my great-nephew Jory, who is eleven and arrived from the Lowlands on Tuesday with one bag and a suspicious expression.

The first wind is the Baker’s Breath. It comes up from the town at dawn in May, smelling of loaves, too weak to lift a kite. It will turn a pinwheel, though, and that is where everyone begins: a square of paper, four cuts, a pin, a bead, a stick.

Jory’s first went to Dulcie Hobb, aged ten months, tied to her pram. She watched it spin all the way down Whin Lane. He did not smile. But he walked beside the pram to the bottom, to see that it kept turning.

volumes.title: The Marsh Sigh
volumes.text:
The second wind of Emberwick is the Marsh Sigh. It comes off the reed beds in the early evening, damp and slow, and you will think there is no wind until you see the bulrushes lean. This handbook, which I, Bellwether Tansy, kite-maker of Whin Hill, am writing for my great-nephew Jory, recommends the lightest thing you can build: a diamond of tissue on two split canes, with a tail of paper bows.

We made one in yellow for Wren Crake, the eel-catcher’s granddaughter, who is seven and lives where the Sigh blows. Her grandfather says it goes up from the punt like a moth.

Jory built another for himself. It rose a yard, he felt the tug, and he hauled it straight back in as if it were a fish. It dived into the reeds. In the Lowlands, he explained, things stay where you put them.

volumes.title: The Ember Draught
volumes.text:
Third in my handbook of the twelve winds of Emberwick comes the Ember Draught. It runs up the river valley from the south, steady as a towed barge, and it is the wind for a long tail. I am Bellwether Tansy, and I was making kites on Whin Hill before your mother was born, Jory, so attend. A tail is not decoration. It keeps the kite’s head up. Too short and the kite spins. Too long and it sulks.

For the Draught we made a red serpent kite with eighteen feet of tail for the Pascoe twins from the boatyard, who are eight and share everything loudly. One holds the line and one runs with the tail, and they change over at the slipway.

Jory’s own serpent got as high as the shed roof. Then he felt it pull and shortened the line, and it came down on the hen-house.

volumes.title: The Fell Comb
volumes.text:
The fourth wind is the Fell Comb, and it is not for beginners. It comes down off the Northern Fells with a parting in it, and it has snapped more spars on Whin Hill than I, Bellwether Tansy, care to count in a handbook meant to encourage my great-nephew. For the Comb you want a box kite: two cells of calico on four sticks, braced corner to corner. It looks like a crate and sits in the sky as if nailed there.

Ours went to no child at all. Mr Prew the schoolmaster wanted one to carry a thermometer up, so that he might learn how cold a cloud is. He paid in full and blushed.

Jory held the line with him. When the Comb took the box up, the boy’s knuckles went white and he began winding in. Mr Prew, reading the sky, did not notice. I did.

volumes.title: The Washday Wind
volumes.text:
A kite needs somebody on the end. A whirligig asks only a post and a breeze, so this fifth chapter of my handbook turns to whirligigs and to the Washday Wind: the flapping westerly that arrives over Emberwick on Monday mornings as if it had read the calendar.

I am Bellwether Tansy of the kite shed on Whin Hill. My favourite whirligig is the washerwoman. She bends over a tub, and when the vanes behind her spin, a crank works her arms up and down. The faster the wind, the harder she scrubs.

We made one for Mrs Suggs the laundress, for her gatepost in Soap Yard. My great-nephew Jory, who is with me for the year, carved the tub and painted the suds. He is easier with whirligigs. They are nailed down. Mrs Suggs says it is the only help she ever had that did not want its dinner.

volumes.title: The Lull
volumes.text:
The sixth wind of Emberwick is no wind at all: the Lull. It sits on the town for days in summer; the weathercock goes to sleep and the washing hangs straight. A handbook of kites must be honest about it.

In the Lull you mend. You also make the one toy that brings its own weather: a coat button on a loop of thread, wound and pulled until it spins and hums. I, Bellwether Tansy, made six for the Hobb children, who had been promised kite-flying and were becoming difficult.

My great-nephew Jory spent it laying out his five kites on the shed floor. All five have dived. He asked what was wrong with them. Nothing is, I told him. A kite climbs on a line paid out, and he pulls in at the first tug. He holds on too tight. He did not answer. He wound his button.

volumes.title: Salt Tom
volumes.text:
Salt Tom is the seventh wind in this handbook and the best of the twelve. He blows off the Grey Coast on late summer afternoons, steady from tea until dusk, and a child could fly a barn door in him. I am Bellwether Tansy, kite-maker of Whin Hill, and I wait all year for him.

This year’s kite was for Captain Marl, who is eighty and gets about the quay in a wheeled chair. He did not want a toy. He wanted to feel something pull on a line again. We built him a sailcloth kite five feet tall and tied the reel to his chair.

My great-nephew Jory launched it and stepped back. The Captain let line out by the fathom, laughing, until the kite was a dot over the harbour bar. Jory watched the whole reel empty. He was quiet all the way home.

volumes.title: The Harvest Shove
volumes.text:
Eighth of the twelve winds in this handbook is the Harvest Shove. It arrives over the stubble at the end of summer, warm, gusty and bad-mannered, and knocks your hat off from behind. It is a poor kite wind and a fine whirligig wind.

Mrs Oake of Lowlands Farm wanted the rooks kept off her seed-corn. I, Bellwether Tansy, and my great-nephew Jory built her a sawyer: a man in a red waistcoat who saws a log whenever the vanes turn, with a clack at every stroke. The crank took Jory four days, and he would not be helped.

We set him on a pole in her field in a stiff Shove, and he sawed as if paid by the log. By Friday the rooks were sitting on him. Mrs Oake does not mind. They are at least sitting still, she says, and she has grown fond of the clack.

volumes.title: The Chimney Twist
volumes.text:
Not every child has a hill. The ninth wind in my handbook belongs to those who have not: the Chimney Twist, which is whatever is left of any wind once it gets among the roofs of Emberwick. It turns corners. It blows up one side of Tanner’s Yard and down the other.

I am Bellwether Tansy, and from my shed on Whin Hill I had always held that nothing would fly in it. My great-nephew Jory, who has looked down on the town since spring, thought otherwise. He made a kite no bigger than a handkerchief, with a tail of plaited wool, for the four Pym children, to be flown from their attic window on twenty feet of thread.

It works. It bobs above the chimney pots like a cork. I should record that Jory did not fly it himself. He handed the Pyms the thread and stood well back.

volumes.title: The Goose Wind
volumes.text:
The tenth wind comes in October from the north-east, and you hear it before you feel it, because the geese ride down it from beyond the Fells, calling. In Emberwick we name it for them. This is Bellwether Tansy’s handbook of kites and whirligigs, and the Goose Wind gets a whirligig, because by October my hands are too cold for tissue paper.

Old Mr Sedge the lock-keeper ordered it. He has counted the geese over the Ember every autumn for sixty years and wanted some of his own for the months between. So three wooden geese now fly on a rod above the lock, and when the vanes turn, their wings rise and fall in order, the leader first.

My great-nephew Jory worked out the cranks. Then he went into the back of the shed with brown paper and paste and shut the door. I am not to look.

volumes.title: Old Scold
volumes.text:
Old Scold is the winter gale, eleventh of Emberwick’s twelve winds, and my handbook’s advice is brief. Fly nothing. Take in every whirligig you can reach, and apologise in spring to those you could not.

She blew for three days in January. I, Bellwether Tansy, sat in the kite shed on Whin Hill with the door roped shut, and my great-nephew Jory and I mended what the town brought up: Mrs Suggs’s washerwoman, short of an arm, and one of Mr Sedge’s wooden geese, found in a hedge.

On the third evening Jory showed me what he has built since October. It is a plain diamond of brown parcel paper, with a tail unravelled from his own Lowlands muffler. The spars are true. It is not pretty. He asked when the next kite wind would be. March, I said, with luck. He hung it on the nail by the door.

volumes.title: The Lark Wind
volumes.text:
The twelfth wind of Emberwick, and the last in this handbook, is the Lark Wind. It comes on the first fine March morning, light and rising, and takes a kite up as a lark goes, a little at a time.

My great-nephew Jory, who came to me from the Lowlands last May, carried his brown paper kite up Whin Hill. I, Bellwether Tansy, held it up and let go. The line tugged and I saw his elbows come in, the old habit. Then he opened his fingers and let the reel run. He let out every yard, and stood holding nothing but the end.

When it was wound down he put the kite in my hands. It was made for me, he said. In forty-odd years I have built four thousand kites for other people. Nobody had ever given me one. Here the handbook stops. He knows the rest.

volumes.title: A Commission from Heron House
volumes.text:
Heron House, Marsh Lane, Emberwick, the 3rd of March. To Mr S. Wickett, Toymaker, Ropewalk.

Sir, I am told you are the person who makes dolls’ houses. I require one. My granddaughter Lettice, who is eight, comes to live with me in September, her parents being engaged to sail for two years with the coastal survey. I have not seen the child since she was in a christening gown. I do not understand children. I do understand houses. The dolls’ house is therefore to be a copy of this one, at one inch to the foot, exact in every room, so that she may learn where things are before she has to find them in the dark.

You may call on Thursday to measure. Wipe your boots. Expense is not to be considered. It is, however, to be itemised. Yours faithfully, Agatha Pennyfold (Mrs).

volumes.title: Mr Wickett Measures Up
volumes.text:
From the daybook of Silas Wickett, toymaker, Ropewalk, Emberwick. Thursday the 9th of March. Walked out to Heron House to measure it for Mrs Pennyfold’s dolls’ house, which is to be a copy of the real one for her granddaughter. Wiped boots. Was watched doing it.

Fourteen rooms. I counted six in use. The rest are under dust sheets, and the drawing-room shutters have not been opened since the old gentleman died. Mrs Dabney the housekeeper carried the lamp and held the end of the tape. The seventh stair creaks. I asked Mrs Pennyfold whether she wished the creak included. She said exact meant exact.

Also noted from the lane: a small round window high in the north gable. Could find no room inside to go with it. Did not like to ask. Three hours’ measuring. Offered no tea. Given tea anyway, in the kitchen, by Mrs Dabney.

volumes.title: The First Account
volumes.text:
S. Wickett, Toymaker, Ropewalk, Emberwick. Account rendered to Mrs Pennyfold of Heron House, the 30th of April, for work so far upon one dolls’ house, being a copy of her own house at one inch to the foot. Itemised as instructed.

To the carcase, in seasoned pine, three storeys, made to lift apart: fourteen shillings. To two hundred and twelve roof slates, cut from the lid of a tea chest: three shillings. To one staircase of nineteen stairs: two shillings. To fitting the seventh stair with a creak: sixpence extra, the creak having taken longer than the stairs. To fourteen doors, hung, all opening: seven shillings. To one front-door knocker in the form of a heron, filed from a brass button: one shilling. To boot-wiping, on four visits: no charge.

Rooms furnished to date, six. The other eight are fitted as I found them, under dust sheets, pending instruction.

volumes.title: The Matter of Dust Sheets
volumes.text:
Heron House, Emberwick, the 6th of May. Mr Wickett, I have inspected the dolls’ house in your workshop, and I write to complain. You have put dust sheets in the drawing room. Small muslin ones, over small chairs. You have closed the shutters. You have shown eight of my fourteen rooms shut up and furnished with lumps.

You will say I asked for an exact copy, and that Heron House is like this. I am aware of what it is like. It is not what I wish an eight-year-old to be given as her home.

You are to model the rooms as they ought to be. And since you will only come back with your tape and catch me out, I have had the sheets taken off the real drawing room and the shutters opened. The carpet has faded in stripes. Kindly do not copy the stripes. A. Pennyfold.

volumes.title: A Figure Not Ordered
volumes.text:
From the daybook of Silas Wickett, toymaker, Ropewalk, the 2nd of June. Mrs Pennyfold’s dolls’ house, the copy of Heron House for her granddaughter, now has curtains at every window and a kettle the size of a pea. She has been asked twice about dolls and has answered twice. No dolls. The child will bring her own, and a house does not need people standing about in it.

I have made dolls’ houses for thirty years. An empty one is a model: sound joinery, and nobody plays with it.

So this evening, on my own time, I carved a lady four and a half inches high, in a grey dress, very upright, with her hair in a knot and spectacles of fuse wire. She is not entered in the account. She is in the left-hand drawer of my bench, wrapped in a duster. I expect to be told off eventually.

volumes.title: A Letter from Lettice
volumes.text:
Heron House, the 20th of June. Mr Wickett, I enclose a letter received today from my granddaughter Lettice, for whom the dolls’ house is being made. I have copied it exactly, spelling included.

Dear Grandmother, Mother says you are having somthing made for me and I am not to ask what, so I am not asking. I have three questions which are diffrent. One, is there an attic. I have always wanted a room at the very top with a round window, like a ship. Two, have you got a cat. Three, do the stairs make a noise, because ours do and I know which ones. Your loving Lettice.

I can answer the third. As to the others, there is no round window at Heron House, and there has never been a cat. I do not wish her first week to be a list of disappointments. Advise. A. Pennyfold.

volumes.title: The Window in the Gable
volumes.text:
Ropewalk, Emberwick, the 22nd of June. Madam, concerning your granddaughter’s questions and the dolls’ house I am building as a copy of Heron House, I must contradict you on the first.

There is a round window. It is high in your north gable, and can be seen from the lane by the pollard willow. I drew it in March. I could find no room inside to match and supposed it boarded over, so I held my tongue, and regret it. By my measurements a space nine feet by eleven lies behind it. I have left the model unfinished there. I can give it a blank wall, as the real house has, or a room, as the real house had.

As to a cat, I can carve one in an evening. A live one is outside my trade, but Mrs Dabney knows of a kitten. Your obedient servant, S. Wickett.

volumes.title: Behind the Wardrobe
volumes.text:
Heron House, Midsummer Day. Mr Wickett, you were right about the round window, and I will say so once.

I went up to the top landing with Mrs Dabney and a lamp. I had not been there in thirty years. At the end of the passage stands a wardrobe, and behind it a door, papered over. It took the gardener and a chisel. Inside is a room nine feet by eleven, and at the far end, under boards, your window. It was my room. I slept there until I was twelve, and could see the river from the bed. I had not forgotten it. I had put a wardrobe in front of it, which I find is not the same.

The boards are down. You may put a bed in the attic of the dolls’ house. I am having one carried up to the real one. A. Pennyfold.

volumes.title: Delivered Under Tarpaulin
volumes.text:
S. Wickett, Toymaker, Ropewalk. Delivery note and final account, the 28th of August. One dolls’ house, a copy of Heron House at one inch to the foot, for Mrs Pennyfold’s granddaughter. Sent by Garrow’s cart in three storeys, under tarpaulin. Loose furniture packed in a tea tin with sawdust: forty-one pieces. The kettle is the one that looks like a pea.

Rooms furnished: the fourteen, and the attic, which makes fifteen. To the attic, with bed, and round window glazed with a watch-glass: four shillings. To one cat, tabby, carved, asleep: no charge. Mrs Dabney tells me a live one of the same pattern has come from the mill, and has been at the drawing-room curtains.

To assemble: the stairs go in before the roof goes on, as in life. The whole comes to four pounds, eleven shillings and sixpence. It was a pleasure, which I have not itemised.

volumes.title: Lettice Writes Home
volumes.text:
Heron House, the 14th of September. Dear Mother and Father, I hope this finds your ship. I got here after dark in the rain and the house was very big and I did not like it. Grandmother shook my hand.

But on the hall table there was another house, a dolls’ house, and it was this house, small. Grandmother said I might look. So I walked my fingers in at the door and up the stairs and up again to the top, and there was a room with a round window and a bed and a cat on the bed.

Then I went up the real stairs with my candle, and I knew the way. The seventh stair creaks in both. The room was there. The cat was there, real, called Tabitha, and she bites a bit. I can see the river. I am not frightened now. Your loving Lettice.

volumes.title: An Order from Miss Lettice
volumes.text:
Heron House, the 2nd of November. Dear Mr Wickett, I am the Lettice the dolls’ house is for. Thank you for it. I have ninepence of my own and I want to order a thing, please.

There is nobody in the little house who looks like Grandmother. I have my two dolls in it, but they are visitors. It needs somebody who lives there. Could you make her. She should have a grey dress and spectacles. She should be sitting down, please, not standing, because Grandmother sits down now, mostly on my bed, to hear what the cat did. Yours truly, Lettice Pennyfold.

Reply, written at the foot and returned by the same carrier: Miss Pennyfold, the lady was made in June and has been waiting in my drawer since. She is standing. I have this evening made her a chair. Both enclosed. Keep your ninepence. S. Wickett, Toymaker.

volumes.title: The Inventory Revised
volumes.text:
Heron House, Emberwick, the 3rd of March, a year to the day since I first wrote to you. Mr Wickett, I enclose sixpence for the creak in the seventh stair, which I disputed last spring and now concede, and some news of your dolls’ house.

It is used daily. The grey lady you made without being asked has been moved from the drawing room to the attic, where she takes tea with the cat. I am expected to do the same on Thursdays, and I do. Lettice has grown an inch. Her parents write that the survey is half done.

When you first came with your tape you counted the rooms of this house, and I saw what you wrote down. Fourteen, six in use. I have counted again this morning, and I should like your book corrected. Fifteen rooms. Fifteen in use. Agatha Pennyfold.

volumes.title: A Shilling in Heel Alley
volumes.text:
Hattie Lask came to Emberwick at twelve with a carpet bag and one shilling, to spend the summer with her uncle Corwin, the cobbler in Heel Alley. He was a kind man who spoke about four words a day. His shop stood at the wrong end of a lane nobody walked down, and since the new boot shop opened on Market Street the bell over his door had hardly rung.

On her first wet afternoon Hattie found a box under the bench. It held odd lasts, the wooden feet a cobbler builds a shoe on, and a tangle of old bootlaces.

A child’s last, stood on its heel, is nearly a head. Hattie gave one a leather nose and sheepskin hair, hung it by four laces from two crossed sticks, and walked it along the bench. She called him Mr Welt. Cost: nothing. The shilling stayed in her pocket.

volumes.title: Dame Crumb
volumes.text:
Hattie Lask was making puppets in her uncle’s cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley, out of worn-out shoes and old bootlaces, and she had one shilling to do it with. Her second puppet came through the door on someone else’s feet.

Mrs Bunce the baker’s wife brought in a pair of house slippers past all mending. They had been blue. Thirty years of flour had turned them the colour of a bun. Uncle Corwin shook his head over them, and Mrs Bunce sighed and bought new bootlaces instead, which was the day’s only sale.

Hattie asked for the slippers. One, turned toe upward and stuffed with wool, made a round floury face with the bow for a cap. It needed cheeks. She spent a penny on red paint, and Dame Crumb was done. Mrs Bunce, shown herself dancing on four bootlaces, laughed until she had to sit down. Elevenpence left.

volumes.title: The Postman’s Boot
volumes.text:
Mr Tibbs the postman walked from Emberwick to the Northern Fells and back twice a week, and his boots showed it. When the left one let in the road, he carried it to Corwin Lask the cobbler in Heel Alley. The cobbler’s niece Hattie, who was building a puppet company on a budget of one shilling, watched the cracked old boot-top come off and asked for it before it reached the floor.

She cut the tall leather into two long legs, jointed at the knee with eyelets from her uncle’s tin. The tongue made a solemn face. She named him Long Tom. On his laces he could stride the bench in three steps, and he had cost nothing. Elevenpence still in hand.

Mr Tibbs came back for his mended boot and watched his old one walking without him. He said it had always wanted to go further than he did.

volumes.title: A Knot from Uncle Corwin
volumes.text:
The fourth puppet nearly ended the company. Hattie Lask, twelve, was making puppets from old shoes in her uncle’s cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley, and Miss Lark, who taught dancing at the Corn Hall, had given her a worn satin slipper, pink, with ribbons. It made a dancer. Hattie spent a penny of her shilling on two jet buttons for eyes and named her Miss Twirl.

But a dancer must dance, and this one only fell over. Her laces tangled. By supper she was a pink knot, and Hattie was nearly one herself.

Uncle Corwin, who had not spoken all day, put down his awl. He undid the tangle and retied each lace to the crossbar with a flat knot Hattie had never seen. Then he threaded one more lace to the dancer’s back, so she could bow. Cobbler’s hitch, he said. Miss Twirl curtsied. Tenpence left.

volumes.title: The Villain Squeaks
volumes.text:
Every play needs a villain, and Hattie Lask could not find one. She was twelve, she was making puppets out of old shoes on a budget of one shilling in her uncle’s cobbler’s shop in Emberwick, and every shoe looked honest. A slipper cannot scowl.

Then Mr Grobe the beadle brought in his boots. They squeaked. They had squeaked through every council meeting for two years, and he could not creep up on so much as a pigeon. Uncle Corwin took off the left sole, found two layers of leather rubbing together, and fitted a new one.

Hattie kept the old sole, which cost nothing. Bent double, it made a long sour face with a jaw that opened, and every time the jaw moved, it squeaked. So the villain was called Squeak. He wore a black cloak cut from a boot-bag, and he could never sneak up on anybody.

volumes.title: The Theatre in the Window
volumes.text:
By midsummer Hattie Lask had five puppets made of old shoes and nowhere to put them. Her uncle Corwin’s cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley had one window, where a single pair of mended boots had sat for a month. He moved the boots himself and nodded at the space.

The stage was the crate the leather came in. Hattie had begun the summer with a shilling and had tenpence left. She spent threepence on red flannel and hemmed it into curtains that drew on a bootlace.

She rehearsed facing the alley, because the light was better. On Monday three children stopped to watch Long Tom stride and Squeak the villain fail to creep. On Tuesday there were seven, and a dog. On Wednesday a carter left his horse at the corner and came down to look. Nobody had walked down Heel Alley on purpose for a year.

volumes.title: Ned Pym’s First Shoes
volumes.text:
The smallest child who watched the cobbler’s window in Heel Alley was Ned Pym, aged five, who left a nose-print on the glass daily. Behind the glass Hattie Lask, the cobbler’s niece, rehearsed her puppets, each made from somebody’s old shoe.

One day he came in with his first pair of shoes, outgrown, the toes kicked white. He put them on the bench and said they were to be a dog.

A dog has four legs and a tail, which means many laces. Hattie made the body from one shoe and the head from the other, its tongue hanging out as a tongue should. She spent a penny of her shilling on a buckle for his collar and named him Buckle. He needed more laces than Hattie had hands. So Ned was hired, wages nil, to stand on a stool behind the crate and wag the tail. Sixpence left.

volumes.title: Rain on the Company
volumes.text:
It rained on Emberwick for a week in August, and the roof of the cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley leaked over the window where Hattie Lask kept her theatre. She came down on Thursday to find six puppets, made from other people’s old shoes, sitting in a puddle. Wet leather dries hard and curls as it pleases. Dame Crumb had shrunk. Miss Twirl’s ribbons had run pink into everything.

Uncle Corwin said nothing. He fetched the tin of dubbin and two rags, and they sat rubbing grease into small leather people until dinner. Most came round. Mr Welt’s nose stayed curled to one side, which gave him a sly, friendly look, and Hattie decided he was meant to have it.

That evening she asked at the Corn Hall the price of a dry room with a stage. Five shillings. She had sixpence. The play would be in the window.

volumes.title: The Boot That Walked
volumes.text:
A theatre wants a play. Hattie Lask, who had built six puppets from old shoes in her uncle’s cobbler’s shop in Emberwick, wrote hers on the backs of bills his customers had not paid, of which there were plenty.

It was called The Boot That Walked to the Sea. Long Tom, the postman’s old boot, loses his other half and walks to the Grey Coast to find it. Dame Crumb feeds him. Miss Twirl points the way. Buckle the dog goes too. Squeak the villain follows to steal his laces, and is always heard coming.

The sea was Mrs Bunce’s blue shawl, shaken from below. Hattie spent twopence of her last sixpence: a penny on tacks, and a penny on a tin whistle for the gulls. There was no part for a cobbler. She noticed on the last page, and sat tapping the pencil against her teeth. Fourpence left.

volumes.title: A Puppet of the Cobbler
volumes.text:
The seventh puppet was the one Hattie Lask was afraid to show. All summer she had made puppets from Emberwick’s old shoes, on a budget of one shilling, in her uncle Corwin’s cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley. This one she made of him.

His head was the oldest last in the box. His apron was cut from the pocket of one he had thrown out, and his spectacles were two eyelets. She gave him a stoop. Uncle Corwin was shy, and might not care to be put in a window. She left it on his bench and went to bed.

In the morning it had changed. On its feet were two boots an inch long, stitched and blacked, laced with waxed thread. He must have sat up half the night. I’ll work him myself, he said. Behind the curtain, mind. Eight words, which for him was a speech.

volumes.title: Saturday in Heel Alley
volumes.text:
On the last Saturday of summer the puppet play was given in the window of Corwin Lask’s cobbler’s shop in Heel Alley. His niece Hattie had spent threepence of her last fourpence on chalk and string, and hung boot-box lids down Market Street reading: PUPPETS. HEEL ALLEY. NOON. FREE.

By noon the alley was full to the pump. The red curtains drew back on their bootlace. Long Tom strode out; Dame Crumb fed him; Squeak crept and squeaked, and forty children shouted every time. Ned Pym, five, wagged the dog’s tail so hard he fell off his stool.

Then, at the edge of the sea, one of Long Tom’s laces snapped. He sagged. A cobbler puppet in tiny boots bustled on and bent over the walker’s foot, and behind the curtain Uncle Corwin relaced Long Tom in mid-air. It got the biggest cheer of the day. One penny left.

volumes.title: What a Shoestring Costs
volumes.text:
After the puppet play in Heel Alley, Hattie Lask passed round a boot, since a hat seemed wrong for a cobbler’s shop. It came back holding three shillings and fourpence, two buttons and a humbug.

More came back than money. Half of Emberwick had stood looking into Corwin Lask’s window, and had seen rows of well-mended boots behind the puppets. On Monday the shop bell rang eleven times. Mr Tibbs the postman brought his other boot. Miss Lark brought six pairs of slippers and asked when Squeak would be on again.

Before she went home she put her last penny on the counter and bought a pair of bootlaces from her uncle, the first thing she had ever paid him for. They were for next year’s puppet. The whole theatre had cost one shilling exactly. A card went up in the window: Boots Mended. Puppets Return Next Summer.
